steps.body:
A podium of gold-silver-bronze cares about order. A **team** does not: {A, B, C} is the same team however you list it.

Those 60 ordered picks contain each team exactly 3! = 6 times — once per ordering. So divide:

60 ÷ 6 = 10 teams.
The six orderings of one team, collapsing into one.

widget.prompt: Of the 6 orderings of {A, B, C}, shade the fraction that count as **different teams**.
widget.successFeedback: 1 of 6. Six orderings, one team — which is exactly why an ordered count must be divided by 3! to become a team count.
widget.lowFeedback: The six orderings still describe one real team, so shade one of the six.
widget.highFeedback: ABC and CBA are the same three people. Only one of the six orderings counts as a distinct team.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 1/6 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 3/6 here — and 1 is less. The benchmark earns its keep later in this course: a conditional probability can sit over half even while a joint probability like this 1/6 sits well under it. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

explanationVariants: Each of the 10 teams shows up 6 times in the 60 ordered picks, once per arrangement of its three members.

widget.prompt: From 5 runners, how many different **teams of 3** (no order) can be chosen?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 5P3, the ordered count — it treats ABC and CBA as different. Divide by 3! = 6 to collapse the orderings.
That is 60 ÷ 3. You must divide by 3! = 6, not by 3 — there are six ways to order three people, not three.
That is C(6,2). With 5 runners choosing 3, the count is 5!/(3!·2!) = 10.

steps.body:
The formula records that division:

C(n,k) = nPk / k! = n! / (k! (n−k)!).

Ask one question before you compute: **would swapping two of my chosen items give a different outcome?** If yes, use a permutation. If no, use a combination.

explanationVariants: Medals, passwords and rankings distinguish order — permutations. Teams, committees and handshakes do not — combinations.
Swap two chosen items. If the outcome changed, order mattered.

widget.prompt: Does swapping two of the chosen items change the outcome?

items.label: Gold, silver, bronze from 8 runners
items.feedback: Swapping gold and silver hands out different medals, so the outcome changed. Permutation.

items.label: A 3-person committee from 8 people
items.feedback: The same three people form the same committee however you list them. Combination.

items.label: A 4-digit PIN from digits 0–9
items.feedback: 1234 and 4321 open different locks, so the order is part of the outcome.

items.label: Handshakes between 6 people
items.feedback: A shaking B is the same handshake as B shaking A, so each pair counts once: C(6,2) = 15.

widget.missFeedback: Swap two chosen items and ask whether anything actually changed.
widget.successFeedback: Medals and PINs care about order; committees and handshakes do not.

explanationVariants: Each of the 6 people shakes 5 hands, giving 30 — but each handshake was counted from both sides, so halve it.

widget.prompt: 6 people each shake hands once with every other person. How many handshakes?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 6 × 5 — every handshake counted twice, once from each person's point of view. Divide by 2.
That is 6², which includes people shaking their own hand and counts every pair twice.
That is 6 + 6 or 6 × 2. Each person shakes 5 hands, not 2, and the total must then be halved.

explanationVariants: 720 ordered picks, each team counted 6 times, so 120 distinct teams.

widget.prompt: From 10 people, how many 3-person committees can be formed?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 10P3, the ordered count. Committees have no ranks, so divide by 3! = 6.
That is 720 ÷ 3. Three chosen people can be ordered in 3! = 6 ways, so the divisor is 6.
That is 10 × 3. Counting selections means filling slots and then removing the orderings: (10 × 9 × 8)/6.

hints: Split the job: choose the girls, then choose the boys, then combine.
Girls: C(4,2) = 6 ways. Boys: C(5,1) = 5 ways.
Each girl-pair can be teamed with any boy, so multiply the two counts.
explanationVariants: Pick the 2 girls in 6 ways; for each, any of the 5 boys completes the group — 30 in all.

widget.prompt: A club has 4 girls and 5 boys. How many 3-person committees contain **exactly 2 girls**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 6 + 5. The two choices are made together, so their counts multiply: every girl-pair can pair with every boy.
That is C(9,3) — every possible committee, with no restriction on how many girls it contains.
That is 6 × 10 or a similar slip. There are C(5,1) = 5 ways to choose the single boy, not 10.

takeaways: C(n,k) = nPk / k! — count the ordered picks, then divide out the orderings you do not want.
Swap two chosen items: if nothing changes, it is a combination.
Choices made in separate groups multiply: choose the girls, choose the boys, multiply.
steps.teaser: Next: use these counts as the numerator and denominator of a probability.

concept.body: Count as if order mattered, then repair. Any k chosen items can be arranged in k! ways, and those arrangements all describe the same group — so the ordered count is exactly k! times too big. Divide by k!.

explanationVariants: 4 × 3 = 12 ordered pairs, and each pair was counted twice (AB and BA), so 12/2! = 6 pairs.

widget.prompt: From 4 people, how many **pairs** can be chosen (order does not matter)?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the ordered count 4 × 3. AB and BA are the same pair, so halve it.
That is 4 × 2. Each of the 4 people can pair with 3 others, giving 12 ordered pairs, then halved to 6.
